ai.title: Peripheral Vascular Disease
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Peripheral vascular disease (PVD) is arterial or venous disease of the limbs that reduces blood flow. In low‑resource East African settings, atherosclerosis, diabetes, HIV‑related vasculitis and sickle‑cell disease are common causes. Diagnosis relies on bedside examination and simple tests, with staging guiding management.

sections.p: PVD describes any disorder that impairs arterial inflow or venous outflow of the extremities. The clinical definition requires objective evidence of reduced perfusion, usually an ankle‑brachial index (ABI) ≤0.90 or a palpable pulse deficit with corresponding symptoms.
b: Arterial PVD: atherosclerosis, vasculitis, emboli, thrombosis.
Venous PVD: chronic venous insufficiency, post‑thrombotic syndrome.

t.b: Is there hemodynamically significant arterial disease? ≤0.90 confirms PAD; 0.91‑1.30 is normal; >1.30 suggests non‑compressible arteries.
Are peripheral pulses diminished or absent? Absence supports arterial disease; presence with symptoms suggests microvascular or venous disease.
What is the anatomic level and severity of stenosis? Detects >50 % lumen loss, occlusion, and flow reversal.

sections.p: The Fontaine and Rutherford classifications are used for arterial PVD; they combine symptom severity with functional limitation.
b: Fontaine I: asymptomatic.
Fontaine IIa: intermittent claudication after >200 m.
Fontaine IIb: claudication after ≤200 m.
Fontaine III: rest pain.
Fontaine IV: ulceration or gangrene.

t.b: How far can the patient walk before pain? Determines stage IIa vs IIb and guides revascularisation urgency.

sections.p: In East Africa, the hierarchy of arterial PVD aetiology differs from high‑income countries because of infectious and haemoglobinopathies.
b: Atherosclerosis (diabetes, hypertension, smoking).
HIV‑associated vasculitis or antiretroviral‑induced dyslipidaemia.
Sickle‑cell disease (vaso‑occlusive crises).
Tuberculosis‑related arterial inflammation.
Chronic rheumatic heart disease with embolic limb ischemia (rare).

sections.p: Patients usually report leg discomfort that is provoked by exertion and relieved by rest, but presentations vary with severity and comorbidity.
b: Intermittent claudication: cramping pain after walking a predictable distance.
Rest pain: nocturnal pain, often in toes, relieved by dangling the leg.
Non‑healing ulcer or gangrene on the foot or toe.
Cold, shiny skin, hair loss, delayed capillary refill.

sections.p: Select investigations that answer a specific clinical question; when a test is unavailable, use the next best bedside alternative.

t.b: Is arterial flow reduced? ≤0.90 confirms PAD; if a Doppler is unavailable, use pulse palpation plus symptom pattern.
Is perfusion adequate in patients with calcified tibial vessels? TBI ≤0.70 indicates disease when ABI is falsely high.
What is the anatomic site and degree of stenosis? Guides referral for angioplasty or bypass; if not available, refer for clinical staging.
Is diabetes contributing? Guides glycaemic control as part of risk reduction.
Is HIV a contributing factor? Positive result prompts ART optimisation and lipid monitoring.

sections.p: Identify features that demand urgent intervention to prevent limb loss or systemic sequelae.
b: Rest pain lasting >2 weeks.
Rapidly enlarging ulcer or gangrene.
Acute limb ischemia: sudden pain, pallor, pulselessness, poikilothermia, paralysis, paresthesia.
Critical limb ischaemia in a diabetic patient.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then improve perfusion, control risk factors and manage wounds.
b: Lifestyle: smoking cessation, regular walking programme, weight control.
Statin (any high‑intensity) – lowers LDL, stabilises plaques; avoid in active liver failure.
Control diabetes (metformin first line, insulin if needed).
Supervised exercise therapy – improves walking distance.
Revascularisation (angioplasty ± stent, bypass) for Fontaine III‑IV or lifestyle‑limiting IIb.
Wound care, debridement, antibiotics for infected ulcers.

sections.p: Long‑term care focuses on risk‑factor optimisation and surveillance for disease progression.
b: ABI check every 6‑12 months.
Annual foot examination in diabetics.
Blood pressure <130/80 mmHg, LDL <70 mg/dL.
Vaccination against influenza and pneumococcus to reduce systemic inflammation.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic PVD symptoms or signs.
b: Peripheral neuropathy (pain without vascular signs).
Chronic venous insufficiency (edema, varicosities, stasis ulcer).
Musculoskeletal claudication (spinal stenosis).

sections.p: Pitfalls in interpreting bedside and laboratory data.
b: Calcified tibial arteries give falsely high ABI; use TBI or Doppler waveform.
Anemia can mask claudication distance because of early fatigue.
Hyperglycaemia may cause neuropathic pain that is mistaken for ischaemic pain.

whenToSeekHelp: Acute limb ischaemia with the six P’s (pain, pallor, pulselessness, poikilothermia, paralysis, paresthesia).
Rest pain or ulcer that does not improve after 2 weeks of optimal medical therapy.
Rapidly spreading gangrene or systemic signs of infection.

faq.q: Why is ABI preferred over pulse palpation alone?
faq.a: ABI provides an objective, quantitative measure that detects subclinical disease; pulses can be normal despite >50 % stenosis.

faq.q: Can a patient with a normal ABI still have PVD?
faq.a: Yes, in heavily calcified vessels ABI may be >1.30; a toe‑brachial index or duplex ultrasound is then required.
In Fontaine III‑IV disease, or in stage IIb when walking distance is <200 m despite optimal medical therapy.

exam: A 58‑year‑old man with diabetes presents with calf pain after walking 150 m. What is the next diagnostic step — ABI to confirm arterial disease and stage severity.

You find a non‑compressible ABI of 1.4 in a 65‑year‑old woman with leg ulceration. How do you interpret this result — suspect medial arterial calcification; obtain toe‑brachial index or duplex ultrasound.
A patient with HIV on protease inhibitors develops intermittent claudication. Which risk factor modification is most urgent — smoking cessation and lipid control because ART worsens dyslipidaemia.

Explain why aspirin is used in all stages of PVD but clopidogrel is avoided in severe liver disease — aspirin reduces platelet aggregation with minimal hepatic metabolism; clopidogrel requires hepatic activation.

A 45‑year‑old with sickle‑cell disease presents with sudden foot pain and absent dorsalis pedis pulse. What is the likely mechanism and immediate management — vaso‑occlusive arterial thrombosis; start analgesia, urgent Doppler, and consider exchange transfusion.

Describe the key features that differentiate chronic venous insufficiency from arterial PVD — CVI shows edema, varicosities, stasis ulcer, warm skin; arterial disease shows cold skin, hair loss, diminished pulses.
A patient with a foot ulcer has a normal ABI but persistent pain. Which test will you order next and why — toe‑brachial index; it detects disease in calcified tibial vessels where ABI is unreliable.
What are the red‑flag signs that mandate urgent vascular surgery referral — rest pain >2 weeks, rapidly enlarging gangrene, acute limb ischaemia with the six P’s.
